title: Flip a Failure into a Success: Improved Bit Flipping Decoding for QC-MDPC Codes
authors: Paolo Santini, Davide De Zuane, Alessio Baldelli, and Marco Baldi
abstract:
Quasi-Cyclic Moderate-Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes are a family of error correcting codes admitting parity-check matrices composed of sparse circulant blocks. QC-MDPC codes have been used for the design of BIKE, one of the finalists in the NIST competition for the standardization of post-quantum cryptography.  Decoding of QC-MDPC codes with cryptographically relevant parameters is intrinsically bound to fail, resulting in a decoding failure rate (DFR) that is nonzero. To achieve INDistinguishability under Adaptively Chosen Ciphertext Attacks (IND-CCA2), the DFR must not exceed $2^{-\lambda}$, with $\lambda$ being the security parameter. QC-MDPC codes are customarily decoded with a Bit Flipping (BF) algorithm.  Especially at very low DFR values, error patterns having a large intersection with near-codewords (which are vectors corresponding to columns of the parity-check matrix, up to some shift) are the main cause of decoding failures.

In this paper, we show how a BF decoder can be tweaked to exploit the knowledge about near-codewords. Since error vectors that cause decoding failures are likely making the decoder converge to the closest near-codeword (i.e., to the near-codeword with the largest amount of overlapping positions with the error vector), we exploit such a harmful but predictable behavior: we let the decoder recognize, and consequently correct, syndromes of near-codewords. This modification comes with a very mild computational overhead and can be applied to any BF decoder. As a concrete application, we focus on BIKE parameters for NIST security category 1. We show that a recently proposed BF variant called $\textsf{BF}\text{-}\textsf{Max}$ outperforms significantly the two decoders used by BIKE within the NIST competition, achieving a significantly lower DFR with a comparable computational complexity.

1   Introduction
Problems arising from coding theory provide the basis for developing some of
the most promising post-quantum cryptosystems. For instance, the three finalist
Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) in the fourth round of the NIST post-
quantum cryptography competition, namely, BIKE, Classic McEliece and HQC,
are based on error correcting codes.
2       P. Santini, D. De Zuane, A. Baldelli, and M. Baldi

    As a common feature of both BIKE and HQC, decryption may fail even for
genuine ciphertexts: this is because the underlying decoder may terminate the
decoding process with a failure, and opens up for attacks leveraging decryption
queries1 . To achieve INDistinguishability under Adaptively Chosen Ciphertext
Attacks (IND-CCA2), the decryption failure probability must be smaller than
2´λ , with λ being the security parameter [1].
    In BIKE, decryption failures correspond to decoding failures, that is, events
in which the decoder cannot correct the error pattern sampled during encap-
sulation. Thus, the decryption failure probability corresponds to the Decoding
Failure Rate (DFR) and IND-CCA2 can be achieved only if the (average) DFR
is less than 2´λ . In particular, BIKE employs Quasi-Cyclic Moderate-Density
Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes, for which efficient decoding strategies are in-
trinsically characterized by some non-zero DFR. To guarantee that the DFR is
ă 2´λ , one needs an efficient decoding algorithm with a sound and convincing
theoretical assessment about its DFR. Even though, in recent years, a variety of
works have studied this topic [2]–[11], arguably, none of these works is a silver
bullet and this problem remains open. As highlighted in the NIST report on the
fourth round of the standardization process [12], the DFR issue was a relevant
obstacle standing between BIKE and its standardization.
    The remainder of this section introduces, with some more technical details,
the QC-MDPC codes used in BIKE, their decoding and the related issues.


LDPC, MDPC and BF decoding. MDPC codes are close relatives of Low
Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes, introduced by Gallager in 1962 [13]. LDPC
and MDPC codes admit sparse parity-check matrices, that is, matrices where
rows and columns have low Hamming weight. For MDPC codes, parity-check
matrices are somewhat denser than those of LDPC codes2 .
    In BIKE, the secret key is a parity-check matrix of the form H “ pH1 , H2 q,
with each H1 and H2 being a sparse rˆr circulant matrix, i.e., such that each row
(and column) is the cyclic shift of the previous row (and column). The resulting
code is sometimes called double circulant. For genuine ciphertexts, decryption
boils down to decoding the syndrome of a moderately low weight error vector,
sampled uniformly at random from the set of all errors with the same weight t.
    LDPC and MDPC codes are efficiently decoded through iterative decoders.
One of the simplest decoders of this type is the Bit Flipping (BF) algorithm.
Let s “ eHJ be the syndrome provided as input to the algorithm, with e
being the weight-t error vector to be obtained as output. The BF decoder works
by iteratively establishing an estimate pe for the error vector and updating the
syndrome accordingly as s ` p eHJ . This iterative procedure continues until the
updated syndrome is an all-zero vector (in this case, decoding is successful, unless

In each iteration, decisions are taken using so-called counters: geometrically, the

the current estimate for the associated bit is wrong and, thus, such an estimate
gets flipped.
    Because of its great trade-off between simplicity, computational efficiency
and error correction capability, the BF decoder is typically the standard choice
for cryptosystems based on MDPC codes [3], [4], [11], [14], [15].

the minimum distance. Thus, there always exist error vectors that exceed the
boundaries of decoding spheres and, hence, any decoder must have some non-
zero DFR. Through geometrical observations and counting arguments, we can

Near-codewords for QC-MDPC codes. A significant step towards a bet-
ter understanding of BF decoding has been done in [9]. In that work, the au-
thors argue that, especially at very low DFR values, the most meaningful events
of decoding failures are due to so-called near-codewords. A near-codeword is a
weight-v error pattern which overlaps precisely with one of the columns of the
double-circulant parity-check matrix H. Whenever the error to be corrected has
many common positions with a near-codeword, the decoder is likely going to
get fooled because counters behave in an unexpected way, e.g., take low values
for erred bits and high values for error-free bits. While near-codewords have
been first introduced and analyzed in [3], [8], [16], the more recent analysis in
[9] explains their impact on the DFR of a BF decoder more quantitatively. In
particular, [9] shows that the amount u of intersections between the error vec-

1.2   Paper organization

In Section 2 we settle the notation we use throughout the paper and recall useful
concepts about QC-MDPC codes and BF decoding. We also recall the vocab-
ulary from [9] and formally define near-codewords and almost near-codewords.
In Section 3, using arguments similar to those presented in [9], we model the
behavior of BF-Max and justify its convergence to near-codewords in the events
of failure. Then, in Section 4, we revisit the analysis of how counters for almost
near-codewords behave: this will be fundamental to motivate our tweaked de-
coder, which we introduce in the same section. Numerical results about toy codes
(QC-MDPC codes with circulant size r “ 2003 and weight v P t9, 11, 13, 15u)
are given in the same section. In Section 5 we focus on the floor, describe how
the DFR in the floor region can be approximated and evaluate the impact on
the floor region for toy codes. In Section 6, we focus on BIKE parameters for
NIST category 1 and evaluate the impact of our techniques on the BGF and
BIKE-Flip decoders, as well as on the BF-Max. Finally, sums of near-codewords
are introduced and studied in Section 7, while Section 8 provides some conclusive
remarks.

we generalize the technique we have introduced in the previous sections and
describe some ideas to handle these more general error structures. The purpose
of this section is to provide some ideas for showing that these cases can be
addressed, even if their deeper investigation is left for future work.

8    Conclusions

We have proposed a technique to exploit the convergence to near-codewords in
order to reduce the DFR of BF decoders working on double circulant QC-MDPC
codes. This technique can be applied to any BF decoder and comes with a very
mild computational overhead. We have verified that, for several decoders, our
approach allows achieving significant reductions in the DFR. In particular, for
BIKE parameters, this becomes especially true when considering BF-Max. De-
spite a running time which is comparable with that of decoders already employed
by BIKE within the NIST competition, the basic version of BF-Max already
outperforms the other decoders (even when improved with the techniques we
describe in this paper). Using our enhancement, the DFR of BF-Max is reduced
further.
    We have analyzed the behavior of BF-Max from an intuitive standpoint, us-
ing simple and crude approximations for counters, as well as through a more
rigorous theoretical approach relying on an adaptation of the modeling from [9].
Both approaches show that, in the event of failure, BF-Max is prone to con-
verge to a near-codeword, that is, a configuration that can be corrected through
our approach. In particular, for BF-Max, this behavior turns out to be more
pronounced with respect to what happens for other decoders.
    Finally, we have initiated the study of more general events of failure by
putting forward the notions of profiles and similarities for error vectors. This
allowed us identifying more general events of failures: instead of converging to a
single near-codeword, the decoder converges to a sum of near-codewords. Prelim-
